title: Migration Amendment (Regaining Control Over Australia’s Protection Obligations) Bill 2013
short_title: Migration Amendment (Regaining Control Over Australia’s Protection Obligations) Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would remove the 'complementary protection' category from the protection visa system.
The government would instead handle Australia's non-refoulement obligations through an administrative process where the minister can personally grant a visa.
The changes would take effect by amending the Migration Act 1958, but the bill does not specify a start date.
changes: Removes the criterion for granting a protection visa on complementary protection grounds.
Shifts consideration of non-refoulement obligations under the ICCPR and CAT to an administrative process.
Allows the minister to use personal intervention powers to grant a visa when satisfied obligations are engaged.
summary.affected: People seeking protection who are not refugees under the Refugees Convention but face a real risk of significant harm in their home country.

divisions.question: The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/debate/?id=2013-12-11.25.10) to read the bill a [second time](http://www.peo.gov.au/students/fact_sheets/making_law.html). This means that the majority of members agree with the main idea in the bill, which is to remove complementary protection as a ground for the grant of a protection visa.(Read more about complementary protection in Australia [here](http://www.immi.gov.au/media/fact-sheets/61a-complementary.htm). ) _Background to the bill_ Complementary protection was added as a new ground on which a protection visa can be granted by the _Migration Amendment (Complementary Protection) Act 2011_. The term 'complementary protection' is used to describe a category of protection for people who are not refugees but who still face some real risk that will suffer particular harm if returned to their home country.(More information about this bill and its background is available [here](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/billsdgs/2990767/upload_binary/2990767.pdf;fileType=application/pdf). ) Australia's [non-refoulement](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-refoulement) obligation, which is the obligation to not return such people to their home countries, arises expressly or impliedly from the [International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Covenant_on_Civil_and_Political_Rights) (ICCPR), the [Convention Against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Convention_against_Torture) (CAT) and the [Convention on the Rights of the Child](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_on_the_Rights_of_the_Child) (CROC) to which Australia is a party. This bill removes 'complementary protection' as a ground for protection visas. Instead, Australia’s non-refoulement obligations under the CAT and the ICCPR will be considered through an administrative process, as was the case prior

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Introduced a bill to remove the complementary protection criterion from the Migration Act, arguing the provision introduced in March 2012 created an unnecessary extra visa pathway despite only 57 applications succeeding on that basis, and said protection concerns would instead be handled through the minister's discretionary intervention powers.

speeches.speaker: Richard Marles
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill removing Labor's complementary protection regime introduced in March 2012, said only 83 cases have gone to review tribunals and just 57 complementary protection visas have been granted since then, and said the so-called New Zealand bikie case cited by the minister had still not resulted in a visa being granted as of two weeks earlier.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: Supported the Migration Amendment (Regaining Control Over Australia's Protection Obligations) Bill 2013, arguing that Labor's 2012 complementary protection changes created a new product for people smugglers to sell, and cited the Refugee Review Tribunal's principal member Kaye Ransome telling Senate estimates that a person's criminal history is not considered under the complementary protection criterion, affecting only 83 matters.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Opposed the Migration Amendment (Regaining Control Over Australia's Protection Obligations) Bill 2013, arguing its title misleadingly suggests protection obligations have been out of control.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, said Labor's border protection failures caused an $11.6 billion budget blowout equating to $1,272 per Australian household, said the complementary protection regime being repealed was used only 83 times since March 2012, and said special humanitarian visa numbers fell from about 5,000 a year under the Howard government to just 500 in the most recent financial year.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Parke
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, citing Department of Immigration figures from September 2013 showing only 55 of 1,200 onshore protection visas granted were for complementary protection, and said fewer than 100 people in total have been granted this protection since its 2012 introduction, calling it often the difference between life and death for those individuals.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, said about 55 protection visas were granted on complementary protection grounds between March 2012 and November 2013, and illustrated the human stakes through the case of an Iranian man known as Affi, who fled persecution for being gay and remains on a bridging visa without certainty of protection.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, said only 57 applications have satisfied complementary protection requirements since the regime took effect on 24 March 2012, and said the reforms responded to a 2004 Senate select committee report and a subsequent review by former public servant Elizabeth Proust commissioned after the 2007 election.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, cited a Human Rights Watch estimate that 14 million girls are forced into marriage worldwide each year, some as young as eight or nine, said fewer than 100 complementary protection visas, only 57, have been granted since the regime's introduction, and described a Bendigo constituent, a 26-year-old Karen refugee who spent her first 20 years in a camp on the Thai-Burma border.

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Summed up debate defending the bill, said the Refugee Review Tribunal remitted 83 matters to the department since the complementary protection regime began in March 2012, of which 41, or 50 per cent, involved people who arrived illegally by boat, and quoted former immigration minister Chris Bowen's 2011 statement that all immigration ministers would intervene in genuine cases.
